title: Who Else Is There Besides Me?
hookLine: Shumbha says the goddess fights with borrowed strength; she answers that she is alone, and all the goddesses go back into her
carry: the many goddesses are one devi
tomorrow: back in the forest, the goddess asks two men what they want. what do they ask?

cards: It's an old insult: you didn't really do it; somebody did it for you. In the ninth chapter the younger brother, Nishumbha, falls.
Even then, another figure rises out of his chest shouting stop, and the goddess laughs and cuts off its head. Now only Shumbha is left, his brother dead, his army gone.

In the tenth chapter he looks across at the goddess, surrounded by Kali and the other goddesses, and throws the insult. In paraphrase: don't be so proud, Durga. You fight leaning on the strength of others.

teach.h: I AM ALONE HERE IN THE WORLD.
teach.b: The goddess answers, in paraphrase: I am alone here in the world. Who else is there besides me?

teach.h: THE GODDESSES GO BACK INTO HER.
teach.b: Look, you fool: these are my own powers, going back into me. And they do.
Brahmani on her swan, the goddess of Shiva's trident, the goddess on Garuda, the boar-faced one, the lion-faced one: the text says they all enter her body.
The field is suddenly empty but for two: Shumbha, and Ambika, alone. All along she has seemed to have helpers: Kali from her brow, goddesses from the gods' bodies, troops from her breath.
Shumbha took them for outside help. Her answer is that there never was anyone else; in her words, every one was her own power, in another form.

teach.h: A FIGHT IN THE SKY, THEN STILLNESS.
teach.b: Then the last fight. They battle with every weapon, then bare hands. Shumbha seizes her and leaps into the sky, and they fight in the air with nothing to stand on.
At last she whirls him around and throws him down, and as he rushes at her one last time she pierces his chest with her spear. He falls, and the text describes the whole world going calm.

teach.h: WHO ELSE IS THERE BESIDES ME?
teach.b: The rivers run in their courses again, the winds blow gently, the sun shines clear. Shakta teachers cite her line for one of their central teachings: Durga, Kali, the Mothers, all are forms of one Devi, the great goddess.
Many Hindus say the same of God: one, worshiped in many forms. It's how a family altar can hold several images and still pray to one.

how: The goddess's words to Shumbha in the tenth chapter of the Devi Mahatmya are recited as part of the whole text, and some Shakta teachers cite them when explaining that the many goddesses are forms of one goddess.

o: the glory of the goddess, read as one long story
a hymn naming every goddess in the battle
a boast Shumbha makes before his final fight

games.q: you're the goddess. Shumbha says you only win because others fight for you. what do you do?
o: say you are alone in the world, and take your powers back into yourself.
ignore him and keep fighting with all of them.
games.why: she says, in paraphrase: I am alone here in the world; who else is there besides me? and every goddess enters her body. only Ambika stands.

practice: If your family keeps an altar, or you know one, bring its images to mind one at a time, whoever is there, and give each a breath. Then let them gather into one, the way the goddesses walked back into her, and rest there.
If you pray, speak to that one in your own words; if not, let the stillness after the battle be enough, the breath running in its own course, the way the rivers did.

wordCard.voice: The Devi Mahatmya. Today, the two brothers fall, and the goddess answers: I am alone here in the world; who else is there besides me?

orig.note: Sanskrit: ekaivāhaṃ jagaty atra, 'I am alone here in the world,' the goddess's answer to Shumbha.

carryVoice: Your line: the many goddesses are one Devi. The helpers were her own powers all along. See you tomorrow.
